title: How to Vet an Instagram Influencer Before You Pay (Step-by-Step Checklist)
seo_title: How to Vet an Instagram Influencer Before You Pay
meta_description: A step-by-step checklist to vet an Instagram influencer before you pay: account history, real engagement, audience data, FTC disclosures and a paid pilot.
excerpt: A vendor-neutral, step-by-step process to vet an Instagram influencer using Instagram's own features, data the creator shares and the FTC's published rules. It ends with a green, yellow and red flag table and a paid-pilot checklist.
content_html:
This guide is for small businesses and brand managers who are about to pay a creator. It shows how to vet an Instagram influencer using Instagram's own features, data the creator shares from their account, and the FTC's published rules. You don't need a paid tool. At the end you'll have a go/no-go decision and the terms for a small first deal.

Before you start: define what a good fit means for this campaign

Write down the location, audience and one measurable goal

You can't judge fit without a target. Before you look at any profile, write three lines:

  • Where: the country, region or city your customers are in. A local salon and a brand that ships worldwide need very different audiences.
  • Who: the age range, interests and buying situation of your customer, for example "parents planning a first family camping trip."
  • One measurable goal: clicks to a product page through a unique link, uses of a discount code, or sign-ups. Choose something you can track yourself, not only numbers the creator reports.

Every later step compares the creator against these three lines.

Free products count too

Many small businesses start with gifted products instead of fees. That still creates a relationship the audience has to be told about. The FTC's Disclosures 101 for Social Media Influencers says free or discounted products count as a connection that must be disclosed. Treat gifted and paid deals the same way when you plan disclosures.

Step 1: Check the account's history and identity

Use Instagram's "About this account"

On the creator's profile, open the menu (usually the three dots at the top right) and choose About this account. Instagram's layout changes often, so the menu may look different on your device.

Instagram's Help Center has a page explaining what people see in About this account, including ad transparency information such as whether the account is running ads. The exact fields can change, so check that Help page for the current list rather than relying on any third-party description. If anything shown there contradicts what the creator told you in their pitch, ask about it before going further.

Scroll back through past posts

Spend ten minutes scrolling back several months. Look for:

  • Niche consistency. Does the creator post about roughly the same topics over time, or did they switch from gaming to skincare to crypto? Audiences built on one topic don't always follow a creator into a new one.
  • How often they post sponsored content. A feed where most posts are ads can mean followers have learned to scroll past them. A feed with no past brand work isn't a problem, but you'll lean more on the pilot in Step 6.
  • Repeat partners. A brand that came back for a second or third deal can be a good sign. Ask the creator what those campaigns achieved.
  • Tone around products. Do they explain how they use a product, or just hold it up next to a discount code?

Step 2: Look at their typical post, not their best one

Compare the median of recent posts with the top post

Creators naturally lead with their best results. Your post is far more likely to perform like an average one. Instead of relying on a universal "good engagement rate" (many published benchmarks give no source, and results vary by niche, format and account size), compare the creator with themselves and with your other candidates.

  1. Pick the last 12 to 15 posts in the format you plan to buy (Reels, carousels or single images). Don't mix formats.
  2. For each post, note the likes and comments, and views if they're shown.
  3. Sort each list from lowest to highest and take the middle value. That's the median, the creator's typical post.
  4. Find the single best post in the same set.
  5. Compare the two. If the typical post gets a small fraction of the top post, the impressive numbers in the pitch probably came from one viral moment.
  6. Repeat for every creator on your shortlist, and compare their medians against their follower counts. You're looking for who reliably reaches their audience, not who has the biggest headline number.

Hypothetical example: Creator A's best Reel has far more views than anything else, but their median is low. Creator B has fewer followers and no viral hit, but a steady median that is higher relative to their size. For a campaign that needs predictable results, B is often the safer first test.

Some creators hide like counts. In that case, ask for the numbers in Step 3.

Read the comments

Open the comments on several typical posts, not just the top one. Warning signs include:

  • Generic praise that could fit any post ("Love this!", "Great content").
  • The same wording or emoji strings repeated by different accounts.
  • Off-topic comments, or comments that don't match the post's language or the audience the creator claims.
  • Lots of comments but almost no replies or real conversation.

Good signs: specific questions about a product, followers tagging friends who would care, and the creator answering.

Sudden follower spikes

Follower history is hard to see from the outside, so ask the creator for a screenshot of their follower growth over the last few months from their Insights. A spike isn't automatically bad. A viral post, a press mention or a giveaway can all cause one. Ask what caused it, then check whether engagement on later posts grew along with the followers. A big jump in followers with no change in typical engagement is worth a closer look in Step 5.

Step 3: Ask for the creator's own audience data

What to request

Only the account owner can see their full Insights. Ask for screenshots or, better, a short screen recording that shows:

  • Top countries and top cities of their audience.
  • Age and gender ranges.
  • The date range selected, visible on screen.
  • Results from two or three past sponsored posts: reach, views, engagement and link clicks if relevant.
  • Follower growth over the same period.

A screen recording that scrolls through the Insights screens is harder to alter than a single cropped screenshot. Ask every creator on your shortlist for the same date range so the comparison is fair.

Instagram regularly renames metrics and moves screens, so the creator's view may not match any description you've read. Audience breakdowns may also not be available for every account. Third-party articles disagree on whether there's a minimum follower count, so check Instagram's own Help Center rather than relying on a number from a blog.

How to check location fit

Put the creator's top countries and cities next to the target you wrote down before you started. A creator with a large following can still be a poor fit if most of their audience lives in a country you don't ship to. A smaller creator whose audience is concentrated in your city may be a far better buy for a local business.

The creator can share a location breakdown from Instagram Insights or from a tool they've connected, such as Instagramaps, which shows where an account's audience engages by country and city and compares views, reach and engagement per post.

Disclosure: Instagramaps is built by the team behind New Earns. We mention it where it fits the task; the steps in this guide also work with other tools.

Keep in mind that any of these numbers come from the creator's own connected account. They tell you about fit, not authenticity, so combine them with the comment checks in Step 2 and the fake-engagement checks in Step 5.

If the creator won't share data

Some creators decline, and not always for bad reasons. Before you walk away, try these in order:

  1. Ask why. Some are protecting other brands' results. Offer to let them blur numbers unrelated to audience location and past sponsored performance.
  2. Offer a live screen share. A five-minute video call where they open Insights while you watch removes most worries about edited screenshots.
  3. Generate your own data. Propose a small pilot with a unique link or discount code, so you measure results yourself (see Step 6). Remember that a gifted pilot still needs disclosure.
  4. Walk away if they refuse all of the above and other signals from Steps 1 and 2 were already yellow.

Step 4: Review their past brand work and disclosures

How they label ads

Open five to ten of the creator's past sponsored posts and Stories highlights. You're checking whether they already disclose properly, because you'll be relying on them to do it for you. According to the FTC's Disclosures 101 guide:

  • Plain terms such as "ad" and "sponsored" are acceptable. Vague ones like "sp," "spon" and "collab" are not.
  • A disclosure only in the profile, hidden behind "more," or buried in a pile of hashtags is likely to be missed.
  • On Stories, the disclosure should be placed over the image.

The FTC's Endorsement Guides FAQ adds that tagging a brand is not a disclosure, and that a platform's built-in disclosure tool is "not necessarily" enough on its own. A creator who regularly tags brands with no clear label is a yellow or red flag, depending on how they respond when you raise it.

Product claims they couldn't back up

Look for claims the creator couldn't reasonably support, especially health, weight-loss or money-making promises such as "this cleared my skin in three days." The FTC's influencer guide also says creators can't describe experience with a product they haven't tried. If you see a pattern of glowing reviews posted the same day a package arrived, expect the same with your product, and plan to control claims in your brief.

Step 5: Rule out bought followers and engagement

What the FTC's 2024 rule bans

On August 14, 2024, the FTC announced its final rule on fake reviews and fake social media influence, approved by a 5-0 vote. Among other things, the rule (16 CFR 465.8) bans selling or buying fake indicators of social media influence, such as followers or views generated by bots or hijacked accounts. The ban applies when the buyer knew or should have known the indicators were fake and used them to misrepresent influence for a commercial purpose. The FTC can seek civil penalties against knowing violators, and the rule took effect 60 days after publication in the Federal Register.

Why this matters to you as the buyer

Usually it's the creator, not your business, who would have bought fake followers. But the FTC's Endorsement Guides FAQ notes that with fake "likes," both the buyer and the seller could face enforcement. If your business or an agency working for you ever buys engagement to boost a campaign, you're the buyer.

There's also a simpler business reason: fake followers can't buy your product. In practice:

  • Treat follower spikes with flat engagement, generic comment patterns and an audience spread across unrelated countries as signs to dig deeper.
  • Ask the creator to confirm in writing that they haven't bought followers, likes, views or comments.
  • Never buy engagement for a creator's sponsored post yourself.

This is general guidance, not legal advice. If your campaign is large or in a regulated area, talk to a lawyer.

Step 6: Start with a small paid pilot and a written brief

Even a creator who passes every check is still untested with your product. Start with one post or a short set of Stories before committing to a bigger package.

The written brief also covers your own obligations. The FTC's Endorsement Guides FAQ says advertisers need "reasonable programs" to train and monitor the influencers they work with. Those programs should tell influencers what they can and can't claim, explain exactly how to disclose the relationship, check periodically what they post, and act when something is wrong. The FAQ says that when enforcement is needed, the FTC usually focuses on advertisers and their agencies or PR firms. It also tells advertisers: "Your company is ultimately responsible for what others do on your behalf." Handing the work to a PR firm doesn't remove that responsibility. If you run or hire an agency (see our guide on how to start a digital marketing agency), build these steps into your standard process.

What to put in the brief

  • Claims: what the creator may say about the product, and what they must not say (for example, no health or earnings promises).
  • Disclosure wording and placement: the exact words (such as "Ad" or "Sponsored"), placed at the start of the caption and over the image on Stories, plus Instagram's paid partnership label if they use it.
  • Approval before posting: the FTC suggests approving posts before they go live, and for Stories it recommends requiring approval in advance because real-time monitoring isn't practical (FTC FAQ).
  • Performance screenshots: a deadline (for example, seven days after posting) and the same metrics you asked for in Step 3.
  • Tracking: your unique link or discount code.
  • Authenticity confirmation: a written statement that followers and engagement weren't bought.
  • Fixes: what happens if a post needs correcting, and how quickly.
  • Payment and usage rights: the fee, when it's paid, and whether you may reuse the content in your own ads.

Check posts after they go live

On posting day, open the post on your phone. Is the disclosure visible without tapping "more"? Is it on every Story frame that mentions you? Does the caption match the approved claims? If not, ask for a fix right away and keep a record of the request, since acting when something is wrong is one of the elements the FTC lists.

When results come in, compare them with the creator's median from Step 2 and the goal you wrote down at the start. Scale up only if the pilot did at least as well as the creator's typical post and moved your own tracked number.

Checklist: green, yellow and red flags

AreaGreenYellowRed
Account historyMatches what the creator told youMinor gaps the creator explainsContradicts the pitch, no explanation
NicheConsistent topic over monthsRecent switch into your nicheConstant topic changes
Typical vs. best postSteady median close to most postsOne viral hit, modest medianPitch based only on outlier posts
CommentsSpecific questions and repliesMostly short praiseRepeated, generic or off-topic comments
Follower growthGradual, or spikes with a clear causeSpike with a vague explanationSpike with flat engagement, no explanation
Audience locationConcentrated where you sellPartly in your marketMostly outside your market
Data sharingScreen recording with date rangeCropped screenshots onlyRefuses screenshots, screen share and a tracked pilot
DisclosuresClear "Ad"/"Sponsored," visible placementInconsistent, fixes when askedTags only, or "spon"/"collab" buried in hashtags
Product claimsExplains real useEnthusiastic but vagueUnsupported health or money claims
Pilot termsAgrees to brief, approval and reportingNegotiates some pointsRefuses approval or disclosure terms

One red flag in disclosures, data sharing or follower growth is usually enough to stop. Several yellows mean a smaller, tightly tracked pilot.

FAQ

Do I need a paid vetting tool?

No. Every step here uses Instagram's own features, data the creator shares from their account, and free FTC guidance. Tools can save time when you're comparing many creators. If you use one, ask how it calculates any score it shows, and still read the comments and past disclosures yourself.

Is Instagram's built-in "Paid partnership" label enough?

Not necessarily. The FTC's Endorsement Guides FAQ says a platform's built-in disclosure tool may not be enough on its own; the disclosure still has to be clear and easy to notice. The safest approach is to use the label and also put plain words like "Ad" at the start of the caption and over the image on Stories.

What if the creator is outside the US?

According to the FTC's Disclosures 101 guide, US law applies if a post is reasonably likely to reach US consumers, even when the creator posts from another country. If your business or audience is outside the US, also check the advertising rules from your own country's regulator.

Do gifted products need a disclosure?

Yes. The FTC treats free or discounted products as a relationship that must be disclosed, so put the same disclosure terms in a gifted brief as in a paid one.

fact_check.intent_notes: Passes, but with gaps. Better than a generic answer: structured around a decision, legal parts accurately sourced, and the buyer's own FTC obligations are rarely explained this well. It falls short of what it promises on checking whether a creator is genuine. The "About this account" section avoids the most useful facts: Instagram's page lists four fields (date joined, number of username changes, "Account based in" (country, based on the account's activity), and active ads). These are the best free ways to tell if a creator is genuine, and "Account based in" is a direct location check. The article tells readers to look these up rather than naming them, so its "contradicts the pitch" test has nothing concrete to compare against. Fix: name the "About this account" fields and turn them into concrete checks.
fact_check.value_notes: Adds some original value. Claimed differentiators present: the median-versus-best-post method, an escalation ladder for creators who won't share data, correct use of the 2024 rule, the FAQ and Disclosures 101, and the green/yellow/red table and pilot brief. Weaknesses: the median method has no numbers (the worked example uses no figures and "a small fraction of the top post" is never defined; add one numeric example and a simple ratio, median engagement ÷ followers). The fake-follower checks are standard and leave out common free checks such as sampling the follower list for empty or no-photo accounts. The link to a "start a digital marketing agency" guide is self-promotion and off-topic for this reader; remove it. Uncheckable opinions/advice (screen recording harder to fake than a screenshot; "many benchmarks give no source"; the median heuristic) are reasonable and presented as advice.
fact_check.product_notes: Instagramaps claims are within the allowed list. "A tool the creator has connected" matches "connect an Instagram account". "Shows where an account's audience engages by country and city" matches. "Compares views, reach and engagement per post" matches. No marketplace or pricing claims, which is fine. The ownership disclosure is present. The article says this data shows fit, not authenticity, which is the right limit. The FAQ's "no paid tool needed" line doesn't conflict with the free plans. Compliant.
